Music Technology | Years 12–13 | October 2026   Page 1

About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Music Technology Years 12–13 of
the New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Music Technology Years 12–13 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Music Technology Years 12–13 is proposed to
be made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under
section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Music Technology Years 12–13 will be required to start using it in Year 12
from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

music production, live sound and event technology, and music industry practice. They
identify and explain core concepts and terminology, including frequency, timbre, noise
colours, and octave bands. Students also learn EQ (equalisation) and filtering
concepts, as well as mixing fundamentals. They understand how musical structures –
rhythm, melody, harmony, and form – are represented in digital contexts. This
includes working with MIDI (musical instrument digital interface), audio, and DAW
(digital audio workstation) session formats.

Music Technology provides students with the knowledge and practices to critically
analyse sound and music using aural skills and technical frameworks. They apply
knowledge of frequency and timbre to identify and address mix problems, recreate
melodies and rhythmic structures in digital environments, and interpret harmonic
information to support creation, arranging, and production tasks. They assess how
effectively structure, harmony, timbre, sound design, and production choices
communicate stylistic intent, how well mixes balance frequency spectrum, dynamics,
and spatial placement, and how live sound decisions support performer intent and
audience experience while maintaining safe, sustainable sound levels.

 Responsible use of AI

 Artificial intelligence (AI) can support learning, research, inquiry, and creative processes, but it may also introduce bias, inaccuracies, ethical concerns, and issues relating to
 ownership. AI should enhance, not replace, critical or creative thinking, source evaluation, subject knowledge, or students' own analysis and decision-making. Responsible AI use
 emphasises the importance of exercising independent judgement, drawing on credible sources, verifying information, being transparent about AI use, considering diverse
 perspectives, and developing independent thinking. In Performing Arts, where students use AI-assisted processes, they should critically evaluate and direct their use of those
 tools, maintain ownership of creative decisions, and ensure that creative works reflect their own artistic intent, experimentation, and creative development.
